persona.name: Rahul
persona.profile: Eight months out of college, one job building Spring Boot CRUD services. Thinks in entities that map to tables and a Service class that does the work. Has read about design patterns and interfaces for interviews but has not used them on anything real, so he reaches for them only when something reminds him of a textbook example. Wants to show he covered every requirement.

assumptions: All spots are pre‑created on each floor at system start
Vehicle size hierarchy: Motorcycle fits MotorcycleSpot, Car fits CarSpot or larger, Truck fits TruckSpot only
Time is measured in whole minutes for fee calculation
Single entry gate, single exit gate

design.tradeoffs: Using a simple map of active tickets keeps lookup O(1) but stores state in memory; not scalable for distributed deployments but fine for single‑threaded demo.

decisions.why: Enum keeps spot model simple and avoids a proliferation of classes for a small variance

decisions.what: Use Ticket object instead of persisting entry log
decisions.why: In‑memory ticket satisfies the single‑threaded constraint and speeds up prototype development

decisions.what: Calculate fee in PaymentService rather than Spot
decisions.why: Fee depends on vehicle type, not spot size, so centralising logic avoids duplication

decisions.what: Assign spot on entry via Floor.findSpotFor
decisions.alternative: Global search across all floors in ParkingLot
decisions.why: Delegating to Floor respects SRP and makes floor‑level policies (e.g., prefer lower floors) easy to change
Requirement limits to cash, keeping design minimal for now

designReport:
Report for the design stage (overall so far 1.5):
- requirement-coverage: 3/4 — 1 of 6 requirements have nothing in the design that speaks to them: "Entry is refused when no suitable spot is free". Suggestion: Add a class that owns each missing requirement, or state in your assumptions why it is out of scope.
- class-responsibilities: 0/4 — PaymentService describes 3 distinct actions, which usually means several classes are hiding inside it. ParkingLot lists 3 separate responsibilities in one sentence: "Manages floors and overall entry/exit flow". Suggestion: Split PaymentService. Pull out the responsibility with the fewest dependencies on the rest — usually calculation rather than coordination.
- coupling-cohesion: 3/4 — Receipt is declared but connected to nothing — usually a noun taken from the brief before deciding what it does. Suggestion: Either connect each orphan to the classes that use it, or drop it.
- abstraction-use: 1/4 — pricing strategy has no interface or abstract type. It currently lives inside PaymentService, so rate rules change constantly in the real world — hourly, daily cap, weekend, ev, validation stamps means editing that class every time. spot allocation strategy has no interface or abstract type. It currently lives inside Ticket, so nearest-to-entrance, floor-fill, and reserved-first are all legitimate and swappable means editing that class every time. Suggestion: Introduce an interface for pricing strategy and move the varying behaviour behind it.
- behaviour: 0/4 — Step 1 of "A car leaves and pays" calls ParkingLot.exitVehicle, but ParkingLot does not declare a method called exitVehicle. The walkthrough and the class disagree about what ParkingLot can do. 11 more steps have the same problem. "A car leaves and pays" never touches anything pricing- or rate-shaped, so it is not clear where that part of the work happens. Suggestion: Either add the method to the class or move the step to the class that really owns it — the mismatch is telling you which.
- edge-cases: 2/4 — The design does not record an explicit assumption about entry refusal and models the failure as a null return rather than a typed domain result, leaving the unhappy path implicit. Suggestion: Add a clear assumption stating that entry is refused when no suitable spot exists and represent the refusal with a dedicated result object or exception instead of returning null.

Mentor's note: The biggest issue is that PaymentService bundles fee calculation, payment processing and ticket validation; this hides three distinct responsibilities. For the ParkingLot problem you need a clear place to compute charges so that changes to pricing rules (e.g., weekend rates) don't require editing a single class.

assumptions: All spots are pre‑created on each floor at system start
Vehicle size hierarchy: Motorcycle fits MotorcycleSpot, Car fits CarSpot or larger, Truck fits TruckSpot only
ElectricVehicle can only park in ChargingSpot
Time is measured in whole minutes for fee calculation (non‑charging spots)
Charging is billed per kWh consumed, reported by the spot
Single entry gate, single exit gate

revisedDesign.tradeoffs: Introducing interfaces for pricing and allocation adds a bit of indirection but makes the system extensible for future rate models and spot‑selection policies. Keeping TicketResult/ReceiptResult avoids nulls and makes failure paths explicit. In‑memory maps still limit scalability but satisfy the demo constraint.

decisions.alternative: Hard‑code all fee rules in PaymentService
decisions.why: Separate calculation from coordination so weekend, cap or kWh pricing can be swapped without touching other logic
Allows different allocation policies (e.g., reserve EV spots) without breaking ParkingLot

decisions.alternative: Treat EV as normal Car and charge by time
decisions.why: Requirement explicitly says billing by kWh, so we need a spot that records consumption

decisions.what: Replace raw Ticket return with TicketResult
decisions.why: Makes entry‑refusal a typed, self‑documenting outcome
Keeps API consistent with entry result and avoids unchecked exceptions in happy‑path flow

steps.note: Calls allocationStrategy.allocate, if null returns TicketResult.failure
Iterates floors, calls Spot.canFit, returns first matching Spot
Creates Ticket, stores in activeTickets, returns TicketResult.success
Validate cashGiven >= fee, create Receipt, free spot, remove Ticket
Lookup Ticket whose spot is ChargingSpot
Process payment, free ChargingSpot, remove Ticket
Returns TicketResult.failure with message "No suitable spot"

rationale: I added a PricingStrategy hierarchy and a SpotAllocationStrategy interface to split the three responsibilities that were previously jammed into PaymentService and ParkingLot. A new ChargingSpot class captures kWh usage and together with an ElectricVehicle type lets us bill by energy instead of time. To make the unhappy entry path explicit I introduced TicketResult and ReceiptResult objects rather than returning nulls. All changes keep the overall CRUD‑style entity mindset while satisfying the new EV charging requirement.
changeReport:
Report for the change stage (overall so far 1.7):
- change-resilience: 3/4 — Added ChargingSpot, ElectricVehicle, TicketResult, ReceiptResult, PricingStrategy, TimeBasedPricingStrategy, ChargingPricingStrategy, SpotAllocationStrategy, DefaultSpotAllocationStrategy, PaymentInfo behind Vehicle, which already existed. 5 existing classes were reopened: ParkingLot (responsibility, attributes, methods); Floor (responsibility); Spot (responsibility); Ticket (responsibility); Receipt (responsibility). PaymentService was removed. If that was a rename, the rationale should say so — the evaluator cannot tell a rename from a replacement. Suggestion: Reduce the wiring: only one existing class should need to know ChargingSpot exists.

Mentor's note: You’ve spread the charging‑specific logic across many classes; only ParkingLot should need to know about ChargingSpot. Move the kWh handling and the ChargingPricingStrategy calculation into the ChargingSpot itself, and let ParkingLot just delegate to a generic PricingStrategy that can query the spot for consumption when needed. This reduces coupling, keeps the domain model cleaner, and makes future changes to charging behaviour easier to isolate. Start by adding a method to Spot (or an interface) that returns its energy cost and have ChargingSpot implement it; then adjust PricingStrategy to use that method instead of directly accessing ChargingSpot’s field.

p-split.text: PaymentService describes more than one job. If you had to split it into two classes tonight, where is the cut — and which of the two does Ticket talk to?

I’d pull the “do‑the‑math‑and‑collect‑cash” part out of the current PaymentService and make a **PaymentProcessor** that only knows how to calculate a fee (using the PricingStrategy) and validate/accept a cash payment. The remaining responsibilities – creating a Ticket, storing it in the active‑ticket map, updating the spot state and returning a Receipt – would go into a **TicketService** (or TicketManager).  

Ticket itself stays a pure domain object; it never talks to the processor. All the coordination still happens in ParkingLot, which calls TicketService for ticket lifecycle work and delegates the actual fee calculation/payment to PaymentProcessor.

p-refusal.text: A motorcycle arrives and every motorcycle spot is taken. Which class says no, and what exactly does the caller receive — a null, an exception, a result type?

The `DefaultSpotAllocationStrategy` (via its `allocate` method) is the one that discovers there’s no free MotorcycleSpot and returns **null**. `ParkingLot.enterVehicle` checks that result; when it’s null it builds a `TicketResult` with `success = false` and a message like “No suitable spot”. So the caller never sees a null or an exception – it gets a `TicketResult` indicating failure.
If the `DefaultSpotAllocationStrategy` returned an exception instead of null, how would the `ParkingLot.enterVehicle` method adapt its response to the caller?

p-pricing.text: Weekend rates start next month. Which method in PaymentService changes, and which other classes have to know about it?

The only place that actually computes the fee is the PricingStrategy implementation, so you’d modify TimeBasedPricingStrategy.calculateFee to check the date and apply the weekend rate. ParkingLot doesn’t need to change – it just calls pricingStrategy.calculateFee and passes the ticket/exit time. If you want a separate weekend‑specific strategy you could add a new WeekendPricingStrategy that also implements PricingStrategy, but the existing flow only requires the change in the pricing‑strategy class, not any other service or domain objects.
Did you consider whether the Ticket or TicketResult classes need to adapt to store a weekend rate flag or apply the new fee calculation, since they currently only hold the basic fee?

No – we don’t need to touch Ticket or TicketResult. They’re just DTOs that carry the ticket ID, vehicle, spot and timestamps; the fee is derived at exit time, not stored on the ticket. The weekend‑rate logic lives entirely inside TimeBasedPricingStrategy.calculateFee (or a new WeekendPricingStrategy if we go that route). ParkingLot still just asks the strategy for a fee and builds the Receipt. So the only change is in the pricing‑strategy implementation; the other classes remain untouched.

defendReport:
Report for the defend stage (overall so far 1.9):
- reasoning: 3/4 — The learner explains choices and alternatives but does not explicitly state which alternative was rejected nor what condition would cause them to change their decision, which is required for the highest score. Suggestion: When defending a design, explicitly name the rejected alternative and describe the circumstance that would make the learner revisit the decision.

Mentor's note: You didn’t state the rejected alternative nor when you’d reconsider it. Mention that you chose the SpotAllocationStrategy interface over embedding allocation logic in ParkingLot, and explain that if future policies (like reserving EV spots) arise, you’d revisit this decision. Clarifying this shows you anticipate change and makes the design robust to evolving requirements.

exit.q1: Yes, the feedback pointed out that I had bundled three different responsibilities into PaymentService – fee calculation, payment processing, and ticket validation – which I hadn’t realized was a problem until the mentor highlighted it.
exit.q2: I disagreed with the "coupling-cohesion" score for Receipt; I think it’s okay as a simple DTO that other services can use, so I didn’t see it as a real issue, but the evaluator marked it as an orphan.
exit.q3: I would tell a friend to study this example because it shows how easy it is to slip into God‑like services and miss interfaces, but I’d also warn them to watch out for over‑engineering the abstractions – the feedback made me see both sides.
